Highlights of AY 25-26 activities included providing support to faculty during an era of rapid change in the research environment.
The Committee had also prioritized supporting graduate students who faced unique and exacerbating housing and other financial challenges this year.
The Committee has outlined proposed changes to its scope, structure, and strategic alignment with institutional governance over research functions which they hope to formalize during AY 26-27.
Subcommittee Chair Wei also thanked fellow committee members, as well as the volunteer reviewers who assisted in reading and ranking applications for Career Enhancement, Proposal Development, and Collaborative Research Development grants.
Proposals were due in January and awards were announced on April 6.
A total of 51 submissions were received (significantly higher than in recent years) and 18 were awarded.
In looking ahead to next year, the Committee noted a need for more reviewers if the number of applications exceeds expectations again.

They also noted a need for more explicit guidance to be provided to both proposers and reviewers, which would help to streamline and improve consistency across submissions and evaluations.
The reports were accepted. g.
General Education Committee (GEC) Report - GEC Acting Chair Stark explained that the Committee was focused on assessing the C2 (Global Responsibilities) and D1 (Integrate and Apply) outcomes this year.
An ongoing challenge with outcomes assessment for the committee continues to be participation in the process, with only between 13 and 37 percent of relevant courses participating this year.
The low level of participation constrains the degree to which conclusions about findings can be drawn.
The results seemed stronger for the D1 outcome than the C2, as students more often approach competency in the D1 areas.
Students assessed for C2 outcomes consistently struggle with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and examining global responsibilities.
Questions from the floor centered around C2 findings and whether they represent a structural weakness in foreign language proficiency within the current GenEd framework.

Chair Stark, Associate Teaching Professor in Languages, suggested that it appears to be so.
He advocated for treating language proficiency as a central pathway to achieving the university’s goals, rather than as optional enrichment for students.
The report was accepted. 7.

The University of Rhode Island College of Nursing’s Accelerated Online R.N. to B.S. program is dedicated to providing an education that will broaden your view of the world and create opportunities to transform healthcare in your own community. Building upon your clinical experience, the R.N. to B.S. program expands your scientific knowledge base, giving you a set of skills that allows you to integrate clinical practice, scientific inquiry and critical, creative thinking. You’ll graduate fully prepared for a whole new world of healthcare opportunities. Progression and Graduation Requirements Students are expected to achieve a C or higher in all required courses. There are no further allowances for repeating a NUR course, and any subsequent NUR coursework of C- or below will result in dismissal. If the student should achieve a C- or less in two NUR courses in a single session or semester, he or she will be immediately dismissed from the College of Nursing. A total of 120 credits is required to earn a B.S. in Nursing. This includes program specific courses as well as general education requirements. R.N. to B.S. Students completing the minor will have completed most of the prerequisites required for graduate study in speech-language pathology.
